episodes.title: Two decisions hiding in every search
episodes.subtitle: Getting in is only the beginning.

scenes.title: Make a prediction
narration: Here are eight imaginary papers. A search returns three of them. You move the third result to the top. Have you improved the search? Take a moment. What would you need to know?
You have changed the order. But you have learned nothing about the five papers that never made it into the results. One of those could have been the paper you needed most.

scenes.title: The first decision: who gets in?
narration: Aaron Tay opens this book with two questions that are easily blurred together. First: why did this record get into the candidate set at all? Think of a gate deciding which papers are allowed through.
This is a schematic example, not a model of a particular product. The important thing is the boundary. A paper outside the set cannot be moved to the top just by reordering the papers inside it.

scenes.title: The second decision: who comes first?
narration: The second question is: why did a record rank where it did? Now we are comparing papers that are already in the set. Admission asks who participates. Ranking asks how the participants are ordered.
Both matter. A good order can make useful evidence easier to see. But a beautiful ranking is not evidence that the right papers were available in the first place.

scenes.title: Why learn the machinery now?
narration: Tay describes learning search syntax thoroughly, while retrieval mechanics received little attention in his library education. For years, he says, that was enough for his work. Around twenty twenty-two, understanding the engine became much more important to him.

The explanations he needed were scattered across courses, engineering blogs, conference talks, documentation and research papers. His questions were practical: how does this differ from Boolean search, how should I phrase a query, and which papers will my researchers find?

scenes.title: What does the label actually tell you?
narration: Now put a label on the box: semantic search. Or vector search. Or neural, embedding, agentic, AI-powered. Which of our two decisions does that label explain?

Usually, the label alone cannot answer that. These terms can refer to different representations, matching methods, pipeline stages or advertised capabilities. In particular, semantic search is not simply another name for dense retrieval.

scenes.title: Open the box with better questions
narration: No single neural architecture has simply replaced lexical retrieval. So the useful move is to ask what happens at each layer. What has the vendor documented? What is your own observation? And what remains unknown?
A true statement about one part of a system can sound like a stronger claim about the whole system. Keeping the mechanism and the evidence together helps you hear the difference.

scenes.title: Carry two questions into Chapter 1
narration: Return to our three results. Moving a paper changes its position. Finding a previously excluded paper changes what is available. Those are different interventions, and they answer different questions.
Before trusting a ranked list, keep both questions in view: why did these papers get in, and why are they in this order? That distinction is the starting point of How Search Decides What You See.

episodes.title: The evidence you never see
episodes.subtitle: Real citations can still leave a blind spot.

scenes.title: All the citations are real. Are we done?
narration: Imagine an AI search answer with three citations. You check every reference. All three papers exist. Can you now trust the answer? Hold that thought. What exactly did your check establish?
It established that the references are real. That is useful. But it did not establish that the answer represents them faithfully, or that the system found the evidence needed to answer your question.

scenes.title: Check one: does the source exist?
narration: A fabricated citation is one kind of failure. A reference that does not exist can be exposed by checking it. But passing that check answers only the existence question.
Our imaginary answer passes. The three references are real within the illustration. We still have two more questions to investigate.

scenes.title: Check two: does the writing fit the source?
narration: A real source can still be misrepresented. In this invented example, a paper reports an uncertain result, while the answer describes it as a settled conclusion. The reference exists; the description is wrong.
Checking the writing against the source tackles that problem. Now suppose we correct the wording and every sentence fairly represents the papers it cites. Is our investigation finished?

scenes.title: Check three: what evidence was available?
narration: Here is the harder failure to see. Another relevant paper never reaches the answer-writing step. The answer cannot show you evidence it never received. It can be fluent, carefully worded and neatly cited, yet still rest on an inadequate selection.
The preface asks us to examine this retrieval half of the system. Faithful writing and adequate retrieval are separate questions. A citation list alone settles neither.

scenes.title: A simple envelope experiment
narration: Try a thought experiment. Give two writers different envelopes of papers about the same question. Both writers describe every supplied paper perfectly. One envelope omits an important piece of evidence.

Excellent writing cannot put that missing paper back into the envelope. The illustration does not prove how any real product behaves. It shows why inspecting the final prose and inspecting evidence selection do different jobs.

scenes.title: An omission starts an investigation
narration: If a paper is missing from an answer, start asking questions. Was it in the searchable collection? Did it enter a candidate set? How was it ranked? What evidence was passed onward? What did the writer use?
Those are diagnostic possibilities, not a verdict about where a real failure occurred. The goal is to locate the decision, using what the system documents and what you can actually inspect.

scenes.title: Why this belongs in library work
narration: Libraries license, configure, evaluate and pay for the retrieval side of these tools. Tay argues that someone in the library needs enough understanding to compare systems and ask which layer a problem belongs to.

You do not need to become a retrieval engineer. You need to keep three questions separate: is the source real, is it represented faithfully, and was the evidence selection adequate? The papers you never see deserve a question too.

episodes.title: Your route through the machine
episodes.subtitle: Start with the question your work needs answered.

scenes.title: Do you need to become an engineer?
narration: You know how to search. Now a discovery tool says it understands meaning. Do you need to learn to build the system before you can judge that claim?

The preface offers a different starting point: your existing expertise, connected to the machinery beneath the interface. This book assumes professional search knowledge and explains enough retrieval to help you ask better questions.

scenes.title: Three kinds of search expertise
narration: Information literacy librarians help people turn questions into workable searches. Evidence synthesis librarians build and document high-recall strategies. Systems and discovery librarians work with configuration, indexes, integrations and vendors.

Those are different forms of expertise. The first two are the book's primary audiences; the third will find procurement and evaluation especially relevant. None needs to start by pretending to be a software engineer.

scenes.title: Three promises about the explanation
narration: The book follows three principles. Understanding comes before detailed mechanism. Examples come from library and academic search. Formulas appear where they carry an argument, with explanations in words.
You should understand what a method responds to, what it misses and which trade-offs it makes. You do not need to calculate every score by hand. Fuller machinery belongs in the appendices.

scenes.title: A product example has a date
narration: There is an important discipline behind those examples: named products are tied to documentation and the date it was checked. When documentation runs out, the explanation should stop short of guessing.

Products can change faster than the mechanisms underneath them. Read an example as a dated illustration, then check the current documentation before relying on it. A product name in the book is not a recommendation.

scenes.title: Follow the evidence up to the answer
narration: The main focus is how evidence becomes available before an answer is written. The book is an orientation to retrieval, rather than an implementation manual, a product review or a replacement for a graduate course.

No prior information retrieval knowledge or mathematics is required to follow the main argument. The destination is practical: follow a technical conversation, interrogate a vendor claim, and recognise a retrieval problem in your own work.

scenes.title: Choose the route your work needs
narration: Reading straight through is the default. There are also five shorter routes. For a short orientation, use the forty-five-minute reading-and-reflection route. For instruction, protect Part One, then read Chapter Eleven and Chapters Thirteen to Fifteen.

For evidence synthesis, focus on Chapters Two and Eleven, Chapters Thirteen to Fifteen, and Appendix F. On this route, Appendix F is core reading: it connects candidate retrieval, high recall, screening and stopping.

scenes.title: Two more ways into the same machinery
narration: For procurement, follow the category errors, failure diagnosis and implications for library practice. Keep Appendix D open as a terminology map. Use Chapter Ten and Appendix E when a system combines or reranks candidate lists.

For curiosity, if you already understand Boolean retrieval and BM twenty-five, begin at learnt representations. The earlier material establishes why lexical retrieval is broader than Boolean retrieval. Choose a route; return to the fuller explanations as questions arise.

scenes.title: Your own tools are part of the lesson
narration: The book divides into three sittings and gives each chapter a reading-time estimate. Each part ends with an application exercise: run real searches in a system available to you and write down what you find.
The teaching notes include a public-access route. Exercises can be skipped without breaking the main argument, but trying one may tell you something the prose cannot: how your own tool behaves.

scenes.title: Now open the search box
narration: Before Chapter One, carry three habits with you. Separate admission from ranking. Separate reference existence, faithful writing and adequate retrieval. And separate what is documented from what you merely suspect.
You already bring expertise in searching. This book connects that expertise to the decisions underneath the interface. Now, to the machine itself.
